extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy, and critical thinking (philosophers, lawyers, educated public learning about fallacies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognising and diagnosing common logical fallacies—especially ambiguous terms (equivocation), composition/division, and petitio principii (begging the question)/circular reasoning—using examples and disguises from philosophical, scientific, and everyday argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of Terms (equivocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used with two (or more) different meanings in the course of an argument so that premises appear to support a conclusion though they do not in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when a key word shifts sense between premises and conclusion. Examples: 'scarcity of money' (currency vs capital/loanable funds); 'the Church' (clergy vs whole body of communicants); 'theory' (legitimate generalisation from induction vs mere imaginative conjecture). Disambiguate terms before accepting the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous Pronouns / Shifting Referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns or indexicals (e.g. 'I') are used with different referents in different parts of an argument, producing an invalid inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that pronouns refer to the same entity throughout. Example: Descartes' argument where 'I' is sometimes the will and sometimes the laws of my nature; free-will debate where 'I' shifts between volitions, actions, and dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of Predicate Meaning (e.g. laudabile)
rubrics_metrics.description: A predicate word is used in different senses in different premises (e.g. general admiration vs moral praise), making a syllogism invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure predicates retain consistent semantic scope. Example: Stoic syllogism where 'laudabile' meant mere admiration in one premise and moral quality in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sameness / Identity Ambiguity ('same' vs 'similar')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Same' (and related words like 'one', 'identical') is used ambiguously to mean numerical identity in one place and mere similarity or species-sameness in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sameness_numero (the very same individual) from sameness_specie (undistinguishably alike). Failure to do so leads to metaphysical confusions (e.g. Plato's theory of Ideas, Berkeley's argument about ideas persisting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of 'Right' (multiple senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Right' can mean (a) a right that others are morally bound to respect, (b) an absence of duty on the actor, or (c) a right to enforce or punish — and these senses are often conflated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify which sense of 'right' is intended before inferring consequences (e.g. that a 'right to good government' implies a right to revolt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity via Paronymous or Similar Words
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments exploit words of similar form or root (paronymous terms) that have distinct meanings, producing misleading inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for shifts in connotation or morphological relatives (example: Cicero's use of cupiditas/cupidus) that covertly change the claim's force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of Technical Measures (terminological conflation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technical term is pressed to cover two different measurable effects or quantities, making empirical disagreement appear as a conceptual error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specialist terms (e.g. 'force' in the vis viva controversy) can be associated with multiple measures (momentum vs vis viva), clarify which measure is meant rather than treating the dispute as factual rather than terminological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/Quantifier Ambiguity (finite vs infinite senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word suggesting 'ever', 'infinite', or 'for ever' is used with different quantificational scopes in premises and conclusion (e.g. infinite divisibility vs infinite duration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether terms implying 'ever' refer to an unlimited number of subdivisions (compatible with finiteness) or to unbounded duration. Example: Achilles and the Tortoise conflates infinite divisibility with infinite time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Composition and Division
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes true of the members of a class are illegitimately transferred to the whole collectively, or vice versa (a term collective in one premise but distributive in another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring that because each individual instance has a property the aggregate must have it (or vice versa). Examples: arguing 'the world could do without great men' from distributive-to-collective confusion; lottery expectation fallacy; cumulative expenses destroying the spendthrift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio Principii (Begging the Question)
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise is either the same as the conclusion, is proved from the conclusion, or can only be proved by the conclusion — thus the argument assumes what it should prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether premises presuppose the conclusion. Begging the question can be explicit or disguised; examine whether a purported premise has independent support or merely reformulates the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning in a Circle (reciprocal proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two propositions are proved from one another, so that each depends on the other and there is no independent ground for either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose circularity by asking for independent proof of premises; example with mechanicians proving equal gravitation of particles by arguments that ultimately rely on the same claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract vs Concrete Restatement as a Disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: The same proposition is restated in more abstract or different-looking language to hide that the premise is identical with the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare abstract formulations to concrete conclusions to see whether the supposed new premise actually just renames the conclusion. Terms like 'nature' and 'essence' are commonly used to conceal identity with the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Nature' or 'Essence' to Beg the Question
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting certain properties to call 'nature' or 'essence' and then treating them as indefeasible grounds to overturn contradicting facts is a form of petitio principii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand justification for treating selected properties as essential; avoid letting asserted 'essences' short-circuit empirical counter-evidence (example: Aristotle's reasoning about motion in a void).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-begging Appellatives (loaded labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying laudatory or vituperative names that embed the conclusion (e.g. using 'innovation' with a negative slant) to force acceptance or rejection without argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and neutralise rhetorical labels that carry implicit evaluative premises. Example: conceding 'it is an innovation' should not be treated as conceding its badness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking Coherence for Independent Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating mutual coherence within a system of propositions as if it were independent evidence of truth (i.e. a neat concatenation is taken for external support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require empirical or independent grounds beyond internal consistency; coherent but unsupported chains may still depend on unproven assumptions and thus be circular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument from Inconceivability (à priori fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring non-existence from an inability to conceive of a minimum or of some state of affairs (assuming that because something cannot be conceived, it cannot exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on limits of imagination as proof; the example given is the historical argument against a minimum thickness of matter based on inability to conceive it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premises Require Independent Proof (no assumption of self-evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise is treated as more obvious than the conclusion and thus left unproven, though it requires proof as much as the conclusion (e.g. Euler's algebraic step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand that premises be supported; do not accept premises merely because they seem 'more obvious'—they may be equivalent in need of justification to the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguises and Varieties of Petitio Principii
rubrics_metrics.description: Begging the question can appear under many disguises (abstract terms, nature/essence assertions, loaded names, reciprocal proofs), and is extremely common because propositions are often taken on traditional belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to multiple forms of the same fallacy: ask for independent grounds of premises, challenge assumptions presented as familiar/traditional, and expose reformulations that merely paraphrase the conclusion.
